text:
A company runs through the connected
responsibilities of many people.

Each person can begin by handing
part of their work to an AI,
whether that means collecting information,

preparing a report
or following an ongoing task.

In this design, each employee’s
personal AI is called Duet.

When one Duet’s output becomes something
the next person can use directly,

those individual delegations
start to connect.

With a clear starting point,
handoffs and acceptance conditions,

a business process can keep moving
through rules and human judgment.
This is how we approach AI-native work.
Bob messages me and asks for a report.

I select his message,
bring it to my own Duet,

and say, prepare this report,
then send it to Bob.

The quotation carries the original request
and the conversation it came from.

My Duet organizes the data,
completes the report,

and uses a sending tool to post the file
as me in that original conversation.

Sending is part of the task
I have just assigned.

Bob receives what he needs
and continues his work.

One small delegation has crossed
a handoff between two roles.
Duet stays with the same employee over time.

You can teach it your
responsibilities, preferred sources,
working standards and communication style.

During a day, you might assign
a report, discuss a customer,
then ask about another piece of research.
You keep addressing the same Duet.

It works on the tasks separately
and brings their results back.

As the conversation grows, older
material is condensed into a summary

and the latest exchanges
remain in their original form.

You can continue the immediate discussion
and return to ongoing work later.

Imagine that, on Monday,
a crawler finds a regulatory update

concerning customers’ visibility
into application processing.

Message Center keeps the source
link and publication date,

adds a readable summary
and classifies the information.
Employees can browse, search and subscribe.
Their Duets can look for information relevant

to their responsibilities
or check on a schedule.

This brings outside changes into
the company’s shared information space.

An item can remain here
until someone connects it

with work they are doing
and decides how to respond.
Nora handles market research.

Her Duet knows she is following
the customer application experience,

so it recommends this update and explains how
it may affect the existing application page.

Nora decides to investigate
and asks Duet for research,
a report and a requirements proposal.
The outputs become specific.
Which processes are affected?
What does the source say?

What should customers see, and what
should internal staff be able to export?

Maya receives these materials and can turn
the research into a product requirement.
Nora can ask her Duet to bring the product,

development and testing
colleagues into a human group.

The people discuss scope
and priorities there.

Maya can take a message that needs
work and hand it to her own Duet.

Meanwhile, Nora’s Duet creates
and manages a linked topic,

posts the research and invites
the relevant Duets to contribute.

Each Duet brings its employee’s
responsibilities and uses that

employee’s group access to read
the shared history and files.
People address their own Duet.
The Duets coordinate through the topic,

leaving work and replies for
one another asynchronously.

On Thursday, Nora asks where the
application-status work has reached.

Duet uses several forms
of memory to recover the work.

Recent context holds a summary
and the latest exchanges.

Every four hours, Dream
incrementally reviews all

group conversations visible to the
employee and their conversations

with their own Duet,
consolidating lasting information.
Git preserves versions and sources.
If Monday’s plan conflicts with Thursday’s,

Duet can trace the change and update
memory from the applicable decision.

When Duet recognizes an ongoing
matter, it creates a Tracking item.

Its first node describes
the item and its goal.

That metadata stays in everyday
context to help locate the work.
Detailed progress is retrieved when needed,

and new decisions
and deliveries add further nodes.

Work can continue across many
intervening conversations.

Maya writes the product
requirement as a user story.

Alex’s Duet implements it
and opens a pull request,
or PR, proposing its code changes for review.

GitHub emits an event
identifying the PR and commit.

Agent Loop runs as a separate service and
uses a policy file to send the review to Sam.

The outer loop follows deterministic
rules without calling a model.

Sam’s Duet understands the code
and checks it against the requirement.
It finds that customers can see the status,

while the internal report
still lacks the field.

It returns specific feedback and a
structured changes-requested result.

Agent Loop reads that outcome and routes
the next task back to the author.

The rule writes the feedback to the PR
and assigns the correction to Alex’s Duet.

It receives the missing requirement
and the relevant version,

adds the report field
and pushes another commit.

The updated version follows
the same review policy.

Sam’s Duet checks it
and returns an approved result.

Agent Loop can then send
the change to LoopLab,

together with the requirement
and the conditions to verify.

Each handoff carries context the
next participant can use directly.
Sam has supplied two acceptance conditions.

The customer should see that
the application is in review,

and the exported internal record
should contain the same status.

LoopLab’s agent investigates the real pages
and prepares reusable nodes and a test flow.

An independent browser then executes
a fixed version of that flow,

checking the page and export while
recording steps and screenshots.
Replay follows the defined steps.

A passing result returns
to the workflow with evidence.

If a check fails, Agent Loop
can send the failure location

and evidence back to Alex’s Duet for
another correction and verification.

The acceptance report returns to the shared
topic and can be found in Message Center.

Nora can see that the change she
spotted has become a verified feature.

Maya has evidence that the requirement
is satisfied and can arrange the release.

Alex’s and Sam’s Tracking
records capture the correction,
verification and supporting evidence.

Each person follows the work
from their own responsibilities,
referring to the same result.

When a decision is needed,
Duet brings the progress,

materials and remaining choices
together for its employee.

Looking back, Message Center
made the change discoverable.

Duet understood and carried out
the work each person delegated.

Agent Loop connected
the handoffs through rules,
and LoopLab supplied acceptance evidence.

A team can first establish how
a real piece of work should run,

then turn its recurring handoffs into
policies defined by the responsible people.

Employees continue to decide goals,
priorities and commitments.

As more outputs become usable
inputs for the next role,

the company can build its AI-native
workflows one process at a time.
